newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Southern Zaire farmers keen to boost maize output.
newsitem.headline: Southern Zaire farmers keen to boost maize output.

text.p: Zaire's southern maize growing region is producing more thanks to improved farming techniques, while revamped railways help delivery, but it is far from becoming a net exporter again.
The region, which once exported to the rest of Southern Africa, has been hit by decades of economic decline and political turmoil.
With demand growing to the south and occasional shortages there likely, however, the sector is hoping for a bright future again -- provided it can attract the investment.

"A few farmers have started industrial farming again with a few hundred hectares each in the past couple of years. It is small scale at the moment but the demand is there and it could increase rapidly with investment," said Chalikos Basile, owner of the Faiki farm just outside Lubumbashi.

Unable to get loans from either local banks or through international agencies, farmers are restricted to financing themselves, relying on inadequate equipment and suffering from a lack of chemical fertilisers and insecticides.
Yields on big farms are five to six tonnes per hectare per year, farmers say.
But the majority of maize is grown by peasant farmers, who even when they have a surplus have not been able to transport it on the roads dilapidated after decades of neglect.
With an area almost the size of France, much of it potential farmland, Shaba's trade in maize is pitifully small.

The region's biggest employer, state-run copper and cobalt mining company Gecamines, imports around 80,000 tonnes a year from other Southern African countries to cover the shortfall from the region's own farms.

"Gecamines has around 14,000 hectares which are barely used, and if they put some of that in the hands of private managers then imports could be massively reduced, but there are vested interests at stake," said one private importer.

A railway run by a South African-Belgian consortium for the government has in the past year opened up lines to one of the main growing regions, 450 km (280 miles) north of Lubumbashi, which produced at least 150,000 tonnes a year at its peak.

"Maize was green gold in this region and now the farmers can transport, they can start to earn money again. We carried 32,000 tonnes of maize from northern Shaba to the urban centres during the harvest season of May to October," said Patrick Claes, director of the Sizarail consortium.
Traders estimate Shaba's total maize import requirement at 300,000 tonnes but figures are sketchy because of the quantity of trade which passes unaccounted for through porous frontiers.
A big blow to production came in the 1970s when President Mobutu Sese Seko decreed that all businesses be handed over to Zaireans, many of whom had no experience of farming.
A handful of the farmers who lost their land then, largely of Greek origin, are now trying again in Zaire's current more liberal atmosphere.
In 1995 a group of South Africans sited Shaba with a view to setting up farms there, but decided that Zaire was not yet ready for investment in agriculture.
Shaba has so far not been affected by the revolt in eastern Zaire but the latest crisis to hit the anarchic state is just another symptom of the insecurity attached to any investment.
"All we need is investment, but without that, increasing our maize output is going to be a very slow process," said Chalikos.
